notes.1a: This was generally correct although some candidates gave varying numbers of zeros after the figures “25”.
notes.1b: This was well answered. The two that were sometimes in the wrong order were the 65% and where there was no evidence of the candidate converting to a decimal.
notes.1c: Many candidates scored full marks. A common error was to divide 50 by 200 giving 25%. 80% was also sometimes given as a solution.

notes.2a: This was well answered. Common incorrect answers were 15 x 10 , 0.15 x 10 or the answer given in words.
notes.2b: This was generally correct. A common error was dividing 150 by 90 giving 1.6…, the speed in km/min.
notes.2d: Many candidates calculated 2.5 hours correctly, but common errors were to then add on 2 hrs 50 mins or to add on 2.15.
notes.2e: There was some confusion by candidates with some giving correct answers, but reversed. Answers of 140 and 160, 140.5 and 150.5, 149.5 and 150.4 were seen.
notes.3ai: The definition of “even” was not understood by some.
notes.3aii: This was well answered, although some candidates seemed to think that “prime” means “odd”.
notes.3aiii: This was very well answered. A few candidates gave the answer 6 or 6 .
notes.3aiv: This was also very well answered with most solutions coming from the given list.
notes.3bi: The mean was generally calculated accurately with many showing clear workings.
notes.3bii: The median was well attempted with many candidates showing an ordered list. A common incorrect answer was 45, being the centre value from the given list.
notes.3biii: Many candidates understood the concept of range but left their answer as “45 – 10”.

notes.4ai: This was generally well done. The most common error was dividing 100 by 0.70.
notes.4aii: This was less well done. Candidates often gave 1.1(0) but did not show sufficient working to gain method marks. Other common errors resulted from multiplying instead of dividing. 32 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2011
notes.4bi: Candidates generally understood what was required, but some gave the answer as CHF 15.60 instead of $15.
notes.4bii: This required candidates to show an explicit method to demonstrate the “show that”. The method demanded two clear steps of a multiplication and a subtraction (in either order) with clear evidence of where the commission figure came from if it was not the $15 from the previous part. Many candidates gained a mark for an implied multiplication, but did not show it explicitly.
notes.4c: This proved challenging. Many did not start from the CHF1544.40 given in the previous question – CHF1560 was a common starting point. Some added back the commission instead of deducting it. Many candidates earned a mark for an implied or explicit division by 1.04.
notes.5a: Candidates often had some idea how to find the gradient, but were confused as to how to do it exactly. The mark scheme allowed for some indication of y step/x step, but candidates did not always make it clear which values of x and y they were considering, and there were often –y )/ (x –x ). Some candidates managed to get to a correct numerical inconsistencies e.g. (y 2 1 1 2 answer but gave it as positive instead of negative. Difficulty reading the scale on the axes was also seen.
notes.5bi: This was generally well done with many correct tables seen.
notes.5bii: Candidates gained marks for the three points from their table plotted correctly. Those with the correct line often just joined those three points in the first quadrant. This meant that in the next part they did not have a point of intersection to read from the graph. Candidates should take note of the range provided in the question and understand the concept of continuity of graphs.
notes.5c: Many candidates did not understand the link between the graph and this part of the question. Many attempted to solve the simultaneous equations algebraically, with varying degrees of success. Those who had not drawn the line long enough in the part above still sometimes managed to get this correct. − 4
notes.6ai: This was generally well done by those who attempted the diagram. Candidates who did not leave in the construction arcs could not score full marks.
notes.6aii: Candidates were able to measure an angle accurately, but some gave ABC instead of BAC . Misreading the protractor as 133 was a common error.
notes.6aiii: This was quite well done by those who understood the term angle bisector.
notes.6aiv: Candidates were able to measure the length AT , but some did not understand where T should be placed.
notes.6av: Again this was well done by those who understood the term perpendicular bisector.
notes.6avi: This was not well done. Candidates shaded various regions, sometimes including the correct one. However if they did not clearly identify which region they were identifying they did not earn the mark. 33 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2011
notes.6bi: This part of the question proved challenging. Candidates were able to draw line PQ as 8 cm but the angle was often incorrect. A common error was drawing the line on a bearing of 050 ⁰ .
notes.6bii: Again candidates could draw QR as 6 cm but its orientation was often not correct, sometimes due to inaccurate measurement but often because it was drawn in completely the wrong direction e.g. up above Q .
notes.6biii: Candidates who understood the context of the question seemed able to measure PR and apply the scale factor. The most common error was 40 + 30 = 70, with no concept of direction.
notes.6biv: There were very few candidates who gained this mark. Those who attempted it generally gave an answer of less than 180 ⁰ . Understanding of bearings seemed lacking in many cases.
notes.7a: Many candidates scored a mark for expanding a bracket correctly. Those that did not go on to score full marks found the manipulation challenging, particularly regarding negative values, in particular 2x – 3x.
notes.7b: This was reasonably well done. Those who did not score often subtracted “a” instead of dividing by it.
notes.7c: This was well answered, often without working. Some took the cube root of 54 before dividing by 2, and others cubed 2 and then divided 54 by 8.
notes.7di: A number of candidates did not seem to understand what was expected of them. They worked backwards from 6x – 10, or missed out stages. Some candidates drew the rectangle, put on the expressions but did not go on to show how they added together to get the perimeter.
notes.7dii: A number of candidates did not start from the 6x – 10 in the previous part, so did not get to the correct answer. A large number simply calculated 50 divided by 4 to get the answer 12.5. 3 − b
notes.8a: Most candidates understood that only a single transformation should be given, but a large number did not give the correct answer of “translation”. “Translocation” is not acceptable, and reflection was a common incorrect answer. Of those candidates who did identify translation, many did not give a correct vector, either giving no answer, co-ordinates, or incorrect numbers.
notes.8b: Many candidates drew the line correctly. Those that did not drew y = 2, lines that were too short, or dotted. A line defined by an equation should be continuous.
notes.8ci: Candidates could generally draw a correct reflected shape but often did not locate it correctly.
notes.8cii: Candidates could draw the shape the correct size but again did not always locate it correctly. notes.9a: This was generally well done. Most common errors were to combine the elements to give the 2 2 answer 15x or to partially factorise, such as 3(x + 4x) and score part marks.
notes.9b: This was generally well done. A common incorrect answer was –4 from 8–12. Many candidates who showed working scored a mark for 2 = 8, but some had difficulty squaring -2.
notes.9c: This was generally well done. Common incorrect answers were 5x and 6x.
notes.10a: Most candidates recognised that they needed to use Pythagoras’ theorem, and very few tried other methods. The most common error was to calculate 25–4 = 21, and then take the square root. Many candidates would then gain the mark for giving their answer to 1 decimal place. Many candidates who applied Pythagoras’ theorem correctly left their answer as 5.39 so did not earn the last mark.
notes.10b: The area of the triangle was often calculated correctly, but then candidates would go on to add it to or multiply it by another number – often 2, presumably relating to each end of the prism. Sometimes the volume of the prism was found in this part. Those that showed working gained some credit for showing how to calculate the area of a triangle.
notes.10c: Many candidates followed through correctly from their part (b) , although some did start again and calculated 10 x 5 x 2. Some candidates calculated it from the beginning and picked up marks even if they had not earned marks in part ( b) .
notes.10d: This question was challenging. Many candidates did not add together five faces, or did not use their answers in parts (a) and (b) . Some multiplied together all the dimensions and others added them. Those who showed workings generally earned one mark for three faces added together. The most common face to be omitted was 2x10, and other errors included 3 x (10 x 5.4) or 3 x (10 x 5). Candidates that worked through the faces individually seemed to get the correct answer more often.
notes.10e: This was generally well done with candidates taking their answer from part (d) and multiplying it by 2.25. The most common error was to divide by 2.25, and the most common incorrect answer was 5 (faces) x 2.25 giving 11.25.
notes.11a: The diagram was generally correctly drawn.
notes.11b: The table was generally correctly completed.
notes.11d: This was not so well answered. Many gave n + 5 or n = 5 n + 1.
notes.11e: Candidates often gained this mark either by following from their answer in part (d) or by starting again, although 500 was a common incorrect answer. 35 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2011
